body.en: Repetition (iteration) means executing a set of statements again and again; Python provides the for and while loops. The for loop runs once for every item of a sequence (a range, a string, a list): for <control-variable> in <sequence>: followed by an indented body. In each iteration the control variable takes the next value of the sequence; when the values run out, the loop ends and control passes to the statement after the loop.

points.en: Loop ends when the sequence is exhausted

title.en: On the board: Tracing for i in range(1, 10, 3)

say.en: Let us trace a for loop with range. Start is 1, stop is 10, step is 3.
First iteration: i is 1. One is less than ten, so it is printed.
Add the step: i becomes 4, then 7. Both are printed.
The next value would be 10, but the stop value is never included. The loop ends after three iterations.
So range(start, stop, step) counts from start, jumps by step, and stops before stop.

narration.en: We trace the loop in a table: the value of i, the test against the stop value, and what is printed.

body.en: range(start, stop, step) produces a sequence of integers that begins at start, increases by step, and stops before stop: the stop value is never included. start defaults to 0 and step to 1, so range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. A negative step counts down: range(10, 0, -2) gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. The step cannot be zero.

points.en: range(start, stop, step); step may be negative, not zero

body.en: The stop value of range() is never reached. The number of values in range(a, b) is simply b − a, and range(n) runs exactly n times.

mnemonic.en: range(a, b) has b − a values; range(n) runs n times.

narration.en: A quick check: range of a comma b has b minus a values, so range of 1 comma 11 runs ten times.
